title: Translate words into events
description: Start by deciding what a single outcome records. Then build the event from the outcomes satisfying the words in the question.
recognize: The question asks for a sample space, union, intersection, complement, or event.
Words such as 'both', 'either', 'none', and 'at least one' describe set operations.

recipe.title: Define an outcome
recipe.body: Decide whether order is recorded. Two dice rolls are ordered pairs; a selected team is an unordered set.

recipe.title: Translate the condition
recipe.body: 'A or B' includes both. 'A and B' requires both. 'Not A' removes A from the sample space.
recipe.formula: or → A ∪ B; and → A ∩ B; not → Aᶜ

recipe.title: List or count carefully
recipe.body: Keep each distinct outcome once. Use a table for two dice, or positions for hit/miss strings.
recipe.formula: (A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ; (A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ

pitfalls: A set lists distinct outcomes once, but distinct values need not be equally likely.
Inclusive 'or' includes the intersection.

title: Count overlapping groups
description: When groups overlap, adding their sizes counts shared members more than once. Inclusion–exclusion repairs this.
recognize: Several achievement, platform, or activity groups have pairwise overlaps.
The target is 'either', 'none', 'exactly one', or a missing triple overlap.

recipe.title: Identify what each count includes
recipe.body: A pairwise intersection includes members in all three groups unless the question says 'only'.

recipe.title: Repair the double counting
recipe.body: Add the group sizes, subtract every pairwise overlap, and add the triple overlap back once.
recipe.mathTex: \begin{aligned}|A\cup B\cup C|&=|A|+|B|+|C|\\&\quad-|A\cap B|-|A\cap C|\\&\quad-|B\cap C|+|A\cap B\cap C|\end{aligned}

recipe.title: Answer the actual region requested
recipe.body: For 'none', subtract the union from the population. For 'exactly one', add the three only-regions.

refs.label: Inclusion–exclusion for two and three sets

pitfalls: Do not interpret |A∩B| as exactly two groups.
The population size matters for 'none', but not when only-region counts are already available.

title: Count equally likely outcomes or use a complement
description: Probability is favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes only when the individual outcomes being counted are equally likely.
recognize: Fair dice, uniform integer choices, or uniformly dealt card hands give a natural equal-outcome model.
'At least one' or 'at least two' may be easier through 'none' or 'zero or one'.

recipe.title: Choose the right sample space
recipe.body: Use ordered dice pairs instead of just their maximum or sum. Derived values often have unequal probabilities.

recipe.title: Count favorable outcomes or the complement
recipe.body: For repeated independent trials, no successes requires every trial to fail.

recipe.title: Check edge cases
recipe.body: Include zero when selecting from 0 to 999: zero is divisible by every nonzero integer. Check that the answer lies between zero and one.
recipe.formula: number of multiples of m in {0,…,N} = ⌊N/m⌋ + 1

refs.label: Independent blind boxes and at least one secret

pitfalls: Six possible maxima do not mean each maximum has probability 1/6.
At least two requires subtracting both zero and exactly one.

title: Choose multiplication, permutation, or combination
description: Ask whether order matters and whether repetition is allowed before choosing a counting formula.
recognize: Codes, lineups, rankings, and positions are ordered.
Teams, committees, and card hands are usually unordered.
Several choice stages can be multiplied when every counted combination is allowed.

recipe.title: Describe what makes outcomes different
recipe.body: Swapping two selected objects creates a different lineup but the same team.

recipe.title: Count choices at each stage
recipe.body: With replacement, choices can stay constant. Without replacement, available distinct objects decrease.
recipe.formula: repetition allowed: nʳ; ordered distinct: P(n,r) = n!/(n−r)!

recipe.title: Remove order when it is irrelevant
recipe.body: Each group of r distinct objects was counted in r! orders, so divide by r!.

recipe.title: Combine independent choice stages
recipe.body: Selecting an attacker subset, defender subset, and support subset are separate tasks. Multiply within one case; add disjoint cases.
recipe.formula: total = sum over cases of (choices for each stage multiplied)

pitfalls: Using C(n,r) for a lineup ignores order.
Using nʳ when objects cannot repeat counts invalid outcomes.
A captain must be selected from the chosen eligible members.

title: Handle forbidden pairs and consecutive blocks
description: Count unrestricted arrangements, then subtract forbidden arrangements. For adjacent objects, merge them into a block first.
recognize: Two rivals may not both appear, two people may not be adjacent, or designated books must be consecutive.

recipe.title: Count all unrestricted outcomes
recipe.body: Choose permutations for an ordered partial lineup or a factorial for all distinct objects.

recipe.title: Count the restriction systematically
recipe.body: For a forbidden pair in a lineup, choose remaining members then arrange them. For adjacency, treat the linked objects as one block.
recipe.formula: both in r-lineup = C(n−2,r−2)r!; k consecutive objects among n = (n−k+1)!k!

recipe.title: Subtract or use the block count directly
recipe.body: Subtract bad outcomes for a 'must not' condition. Keep the block count for a 'must be consecutive' condition.

pitfalls: A block has internal arrangements: multiply by k! when its members may be reordered.
Selecting both rivals does not determine their positions; arrange the whole selected lineup.

title: Extract a coefficient from a product
description: Find all pairs of powers that add to the target exponent and add their coefficient products.
recognize: The question asks for the coefficient of xᵏ in a product of binomial powers.

recipe.title: Expand only needed terms
recipe.body: You do not need the full polynomials. For x², keep constant, x, and x² terms.

recipe.title: Track signs
recipe.body: A term selected from (1−x)ᵐ has a negative sign when its exponent is odd.

recipe.title: Combine powers adding to the target
recipe.body: For x² use x²·1, x·x, and 1·x², then add their contributions.

pitfalls: The x·x cross term is essential.
Odd powers from (1−x)ᵐ carry a minus sign.

title: Restrict the sample space for 'given that'
description: The event after the vertical bar becomes the denominator. Count only outcomes consistent with the information supplied.
recognize: The wording says 'given', 'among', or 'conditional on'.
The requested event may already imply the conditioning event.

recipe.title: Name the target and the given event
recipe.body: Write A for what you want and B for what you know. The denominator is B, even when the sentence mentions A first.

recipe.title: Find outcomes satisfying both
recipe.body: The numerator is A∩B. If A is a subset of B, it is simply A.

recipe.title: Divide by the restricted total
recipe.body: For equally likely outcomes you may divide favorable counts within B by the total count in B.

refs.label: At least one 6 gives 11 ordered outcomes

pitfalls: P(A|B) generally differs from P(B|A).
The old sample-space denominator is inappropriate once information is given.

title: Test independence and multiply probabilities
description: Independence means that knowing one event occurred does not change the probability of the other.
recognize: The question states independent trials, asks whether events are independent, or contrasts pairwise and mutual independence.

recipe.title: Find the marginal probabilities
recipe.body: Calculate P(A) and P(B) using all outcomes, not conditional totals.

recipe.title: Compare the joint probability with the product
recipe.body: Equality proves independence for two events. Inequality proves dependence.

recipe.title: Use multiplication only when justified
recipe.body: For independent trials, multiply their individual probabilities. For three mutually independent events, all pairwise equalities and the triple equality are required.

recipe.title: Interpret carefully
recipe.body: Disjoint positive-probability events are dependent. An association in observational data alone does not prove cause and effect.

refs.label: When disjoint events can be independent

pitfalls: Pairwise independence alone does not establish mutual independence.
Do not multiply dependent draw probabilities without updating the second probability.

title: Follow a tree, total the evidence, then use Bayes
description: Bayes reverses the direction from 'evidence given cause' to 'cause given evidence'. Multiply along each branch, add all evidence branches, and divide.
recognize: You know source shares or prevalence and an error/detection rate for each source.
The question reveals an error, defect, positive result, or flag and asks where it came from.

recipe.title: Identify the source groups and priors
recipe.body: The groups must cover the population without overlapping. Their shares sum to one.

recipe.title: Multiply along each evidence path
recipe.body: A joint path needs every event on that path to occur. A detection path can require source, defect, then detection.

recipe.title: Add every way to observe the evidence
recipe.body: The denominator includes evidence from the target group and all other groups.

recipe.title: Take the target share of the evidence
recipe.body: Divide the target evidence branch by the total evidence probability. Expected-frequency tables offer the same calculation using counts.

refs.label: Total probability and general Bayes’ rule

pitfalls: Sensitivity is P(positive|disease), not P(disease|positive).
Specificity is P(negative|no disease); its complement is the false-positive rate.
Conditionally independent repeated tests must be multiplied within each true-status group, then Bayes applied.

title: Build a discrete distribution and transform values
description: A random variable maps outcomes to numbers. For a transformed value, add probabilities of all original values that map to it.
recognize: The question asks for a range, a PMF normalization constant, or the probability of Y=g(X).

recipe.title: List possible original values
recipe.body: Count what X measures and its smallest and largest feasible values.

recipe.title: Normalize or compute masses
recipe.body: A valid discrete PMF has nonnegative probabilities that sum to one. Independent success counts have C(n,k) ways to place k successes.

recipe.title: Map each value if a transformation is given
recipe.body: Make a small table x→g(x). Repeated transformed values appear only once in the range.
recipe.formula: range of Y = {g(x): x in range of X}

recipe.title: Add all matching masses
recipe.body: If two original values produce the same target, include both probabilities.

refs.label: Different outcomes can have the same value

pitfalls: Do not include impossible values in the range.
A square transformation is often many-to-one.
Normalize before adding the requested masses.

title: Read a CDF using endpoints and jumps
description: A CDF accumulates probability up to and including its input. A jump at a discrete value gives the probability at that value.
recognize: F(x)=P(X≤x) is supplied, or a question asks whether a function can be a CDF.

recipe.title: Decode the inequality
recipe.body: The CDF includes its upper endpoint. A strict lower endpoint is removed by subtracting F at that lower value.

recipe.title: Read point masses from jumps
recipe.body: For a discrete distribution use the value just before the jump, written F(x−).

recipe.title: Condition if information is given
recipe.body: After finding the event mass, divide by the mass of the given event.

recipe.title: Check validity
recipe.body: A CDF is nondecreasing, right-continuous, and tends to zero at the left end and one at the right end.

refs.label: Definition of the cumulative distribution function
CDF properties: monotonicity, right-continuity, and limits

pitfalls: P(X≥1) is 1−F(1−), not generally 1−F(1).
A CDF may have flat parts and jumps; it may never decrease.

title: Wait for the first success
description: Independent trials with a constant success probability give a geometric waiting time counted from trial one.
recognize: The variable is the number of attempts until the first defect, rare item, or success.
The question asks 'by attempt n', an interval, or how many attempts meet a target probability.

recipe.title: Identify p and the failure probability
recipe.body: Check independent trials and an unchanged success probability. Set q=1−p.

recipe.title: Choose point, tail, or interval
recipe.body: First success on n requires n−1 failures then success. No success after n requires all n failures.

recipe.title: Use remaining attempts after known failures
recipe.body: Past failures do not affect future independent trials. Subtract the completed attempts from the deadline.

recipe.title: Solve a target inequality
recipe.body: Take logarithms and reverse the inequality when dividing by the negative number log(q). Round up and check the neighboring integer.

refs.label: Waiting for the first defect: PMF and by-n probability

pitfalls: Exactly the nth trial and by the nth trial are different events.
A guarantee or changing chance breaks the ordinary geometric model.
After m known failures, a deadline of n leaves n−m attempts.

title: Count categories in a sample
description: Without replacement, count unordered samples using combinations. With replacement, independent draws can use the binomial formula.
recognize: A fixed finite batch contains known category counts and a fixed-size sample is drawn.

recipe.title: Identify the population and the sample
recipe.body: Let N be the population, K the target-category count, and n the sample size.
recipe.formula: N, K, n; feasible x: max(0,n−(N−K)) ≤ x ≤ min(n,K)

recipe.title: Count favorable unordered samples
recipe.body: Choose x target objects and n−x other objects. Multiply the two choice counts.

recipe.title: Divide by all samples
recipe.body: All n-element subsets are equally likely under uniform sampling without replacement.

recipe.title: Adjust for replacement or conditioning
recipe.body: Replacement restores the category chance on each draw; no replacement changes it. For a given event, restrict and divide again.

pitfalls: Without replacement, the draws are generally dependent.
Use the same counting convention in numerator and denominator.

title: Recover probabilities from disjoint pieces
description: Break events into disjoint regions. Their probabilities add; subtract known pieces to recover unknown masses.
recognize: Probabilities of overlapping events and their intersection are supplied.
The sample-space outcomes are not equally likely, so counting alone cannot give event probabilities.

recipe.title: Identify disjoint pieces
recipe.body: Separate an event into its shared and unshared parts. For singleton outcomes, identify which outcome is the intersection.

recipe.title: Subtract known probability
recipe.body: The total event mass equals the sum of its disjoint parts, so remove a known part to obtain the other.

recipe.title: Add the target pieces
recipe.body: Add only regions that are disjoint. For a union that overlaps, subtract its intersection once.

recipe.title: Check normalization
recipe.body: All singleton masses in a finite sample space must be nonnegative and sum to one.

pitfalls: Do not assign equal masses merely because there are finitely many outcomes.
Adding overlapping event probabilities without subtracting the overlap double counts its mass.
